content:
Around 90,000 hip replacements are performed annually in the UK. It is one of the most reliable operations for relieving arthritis pain, with over 90% of patients reporting excellent results lasting 15-25+ years.

Quick answer: Hip replacement is recommended when severe hip pain impacts daily life and non-surgical treatments have failed. Over 90% of patients experience excellent results lasting 15-25+ years. There are two main types: total hip replacement and hip resurfacing. Recovery typically involves using crutches for 6 weeks, with full benefits usually seen after 12 months, alongside following specific hip precautions.

When Is Hip Replacement Recommended?

  • Severe hip pain affecting sleep, walking, and quality of life
  • Non-surgical treatments have been exhausted (physiotherapy, injections, weight management)
  • X-rays show significant joint damage
  • Difficulty with daily tasks like putting on shoes, climbing stairs, or getting in and out of a car

Types of Hip Replacement

  • Total hip replacement (THR) — both ball and socket are replaced. Most common.
  • Hip resurfacing — the bone is trimmed and capped rather than removed. Less common, sometimes offered to younger patients.
  • Anterior approach — newer technique through the front of the hip. Potentially faster recovery but not available everywhere.

The NHS Process

  1. GP referral to orthopaedic surgeon
  2. Consultation and X-rays
  3. Pre-operative assessment (blood tests, general health check)
  4. Surgery — usually 1-2 hours under spinal anaesthetic
  5. Hospital stay — typically 1-3 days
  6. Follow-up at 6 weeks and 1 year

Recovery Timeline

  • Day 1 — you'll be helped to stand and take steps with a frame
  • Weeks 1-6 — walking with crutches, following hip precautions
  • Week 6 — most people can start driving (if automatic car)
  • Weeks 6-12 — increasing activity, many return to work (desk jobs)
  • 3-6 months — significant improvement, most restrictions lifted
  • 12 months — full benefit usually achieved

Hip Precautions

After surgery, you'll need to follow precautions to prevent dislocation:

  • Don't cross your legs
  • Don't bend your hip past 90 degrees
  • Don't twist your leg inward
  • Use a raised toilet seat and shower seat
  • Sleep on your back or non-operated side with a pillow between your knees

Preparing Your Home

  • Remove trip hazards (loose rugs, trailing cables)
  • Arrange a bed on the ground floor if possible
  • Stock up on easy-to-prepare meals
  • Install grab rails in the bathroom
  • Arrange help for the first 2-3 weeks after surgery

Hip replacement is a life-changing operation for many people with arthritis. Discuss all your options with your surgeon and commit to physiotherapy for the best possible outcome.

Practical next steps for Hip Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide

If you came here about Hip Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Quick questions about Replacement Arthritis Guide

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
